mcqs.question: A Next.js App Router file starts with `'use client'`. Which statement is accurate?
options: The component is excluded from server rendering and only runs in the browser
The directive marks a module-graph boundary: the component still renders to HTML on the server, and its imports join the client bundle
The directive turns the component into a Server Component with client privileges
The directive disables hydration for that subtree to avoid mismatches
mcqs.explanation: `'use client'` declares where the server module graph ends: the file and its imports become client code, but Client Components are still server-rendered into the initial HTML and hydrated, which is why state, Effects, and event handlers are allowed only below the boundary (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components). The strongest distractor is option 0, the most common misconception: browser-only rendering would break SSR entirely; the directive controls what ships to the browser, not where the component renders.

mcqs.question: When does an OnPush component re-render in modern Angular?
options: When its inputs change or when a signal it reads in the template updates
On every DOM event anywhere in the application
Only when the router navigates
Whenever any service field changes
mcqs.explanation: OnPush marks the component dirty only for input reference changes or tracked signal updates; signal tracking makes the dependency set explicit instead of invalidating broadly.

mcqs.question: A Client Component imports a function from a module that starts with `'use server'`. Which statement about the import is accurate?
options: The import is bundled into the client and runs in the browser; the directive only blocks accidental Node.js APIs.
The call becomes a request to the server: the function must authenticate and authorize the caller and validate its arguments, because the boundary is reachable by any caller.
The directive makes the function private to the importing module, so an internal authorization check is optional.
The directive is also applied inside `proxy`, so an authorization redirect there protects the function.
mcqs.explanation: `'use server'` marks a server entry point, not a private helper: the Client Component receives a framework-managed reference and every call crosses a network boundary, so the function is the security boundary and must check the session itself and validate each argument (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server). Option 2 is the strongest distractor — "server" reads as "internal", but a hidden button or a private import changes nothing about who can reach the endpoint. Option 3 is wrong on a documented point: `proxy` does not transform `'use server'`, so the function runs normally there and the redirect is only an optimistic pre-check.

mcqs.question: Cache Components is enabled. After a user saves an edit, that same user must see the new value on the next read. Which invalidation matches the documented behaviour?
options: `revalidateTag('products')` — it invalidates the tagged entries, so the next read comes back fresh.
`updateTag('products')` — it invalidates the tagged scope for immediate read-your-own-writes.
`cacheLife('seconds')` — it shortens the lifetime so the next read recomputes.
`{ cache: 'no-store' }` on the `fetch` — it bypasses the cache for that request.
mcqs.explanation: In the Cache Components model a tag is an invalidation label, not a freshness period: `revalidateTag` invalidates with stale-while-revalidate semantics, while `updateTag` is the documented call for immediate read-your-own-writes (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating). Option 0 is the strongest distractor because it is the right call for the opposite requirement — with it the user who just saved can still receive the stale entry while the refresh happens, which is exactly the complaint. Option 2 is a lifetime hint rather than an invalidation key, and option 3 is previous-model `fetch` vocabulary that does not invalidate anything for other readers.

mcqs.question: A catalog page is identical for every visitor except an account menu that reads `cookies()`. With Cache Components, how do you keep the page prerenderable without breaking personalization?
options: Read the cookie at the top of the page so the whole route renders per request.
Keep the page out of request scope and put only the account menu behind a `Suspense` boundary whose fallback is part of the shell.
Wrap the entire page in one `Suspense` with a spinner fallback, then read the cookie anywhere.
Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to the root layout so the account menu is always correct.
mcqs.explanation: Partial Prerendering builds a static shell and streams the request-dependent work behind `Suspense`: the fallback ships in the shell and the live account data arrives later, so the stable catalog stays cacheable and CDN-servable (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/caching). Option 0 is the strongest distractor — it is correct about the data and wrong about the shape of the route: one leaf reading the request turns the entire route request-time, which is the blanket label the decision rule rejects. Option 2 also makes the whole page request-dependent and streams a shell with no content, and option 3 applies the same mistake at the widest possible scope with the previous-model route switch.

mcqs.question: An interactive subtree needs a theme context that also holds client state, while the content it renders is fetched on the server. Which structure preserves both?
options: Mark the page `'use client'`, create the context at its top, and fetch the data in an Effect.
Make the provider a Client Component and pass the server-rendered subtree as `children`; the server tree keeps rendering on the server.
Call `createContext` in the Server Component and consume it from the Client Component below.
Store the data in a module-level singleton imported by both the server and the client module.
mcqs.explanation: The provider must be a Client Component because it owns state and context, but `children` already holds rendered server output passed as a prop, so nothing below the provider is forced into the client bundle (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components). Option 0 is the strongest distractor because it runs: that is the trap, since it converts the page and its data fetching into client code. Option 2 is invalid because Server Components cannot use React context, and option 3 treats a shared module as transport — server module state is not a per-request channel to the browser and leaks across requests.

mcqs.question: `/admin` is protected by a redirect in `proxy` and by an auth check in its layout. A Server Function in the same area deletes records. What is missing?
options: Nothing: `proxy` runs before the request and the layout gates every child page.
Authorization inside the function itself: layouts can persist across client navigations and `proxy` is only an optimistic pre-check.
Nothing, as long as the session cookie is `httpOnly` and `secure`.
A matcher in `proxy` that also covers the Server Function endpoint.
mcqs.explanation: Authorization has to be enforced where the data is touched: a layout can survive a client navigation without re-running, and the redirect in `proxy` is a pre-check rather than a security boundary, so the mutation must repeat the check (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication). Option 0 is the strongest distractor because both checks look like enforcement and neither sits next to the delete. Option 2 confuses theft protection with authorization — `httpOnly`/`secure` protect the cookie, they do not decide what the caller may delete — and option 3 only widens the same optimistic pre-check: a matcher decides where `proxy` runs, not who may call the function.

mcqs.question: A feature route must exist only while its feature flag is on; when the flag is off, the router should keep looking at the remaining route configurations. Which guard fits?
options: `canActivate` returning `false`.
`canMatch` returning `false`.
`canDeactivate` returning `false`.
`canActivateChild` returning `false`.
mcqs.explanation: `canMatch` decides whether a route configuration participates in matching at all, so `false` skips it and the router continues with the next candidate — the documented tool for conditional matching such as feature flags (https://angular.dev/guide/routing/route-guards). Option 0 is the strongest distractor because both guards look like "block access"; the difference is timing: `canActivate` runs after the route already matched and cancels the navigation instead of trying another configuration. `canDeactivate` is about leaving a route with unsaved work, and `canActivateChild` still depends on its parent having matched.

mcqs.question: A component exposes `results = toSignal(results$, { initialValue: [] })`, where `results$` is `query$` piped through `debounceTime(200)` and `switchMap` into HTTP. A teammate proposes replacing the pipeline with a signal plus `computed`. What is the correct response?
options: Good: `computed` cancels in-flight requests the way `switchMap` does, so the pipeline is redundant.
Keep the async pipeline in RxJS and expose the view value as a signal; `computed` cannot express debounce or cancellation.
The current code is broken: `toSignal` only accepts synchronous Observables.
Signals cannot feed a template without `async`, so the current code will not render.
mcqs.explanation: Signals model synchronous current state and memoized derivation; time-based operators and switching between in-flight requests belong to RxJS, with `toSignal`/`toObservable` as the deliberate bridge (https://angular.dev/ecosystem/rxjs-interop). Option 0 is the strongest distractor because `computed` also caches, but it is lazy and synchronous: it has no notion of a sequence over time, so it cannot debounce or cancel. Option 2 is false because `toSignal` subscribes to any Observable, and option 3 reverses Angular's template model, where signals are read directly.

scenarios.prompt: This Next.js App Router dashboard fails at runtime and its client bundle is larger than expected. Diagnose each problem and restructure the tree.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Problem 1: Chart.tsx calls useState but has no 'use client' directive, so it runs as a Server Component, where interactive state is not available; the page fails at runtime. Add 'use client' at the top of Chart.tsx. The directive is a module-graph boundary: Chart and its chart-library imports join the client bundle, which is why placement should be as low in the tree as practical to limit JavaScript. Problem 2: `onRefresh={() => db.metrics.findMany()}` crosses the server-to-client boundary as a prop, and props crossing that boundary must be serializable; an ordinary function closure is not. The supported crossing is a Server Function marked with 'use server', which the framework passes to the client as a callable reference. Alternatives: trigger revalidation from the client (a client-side refresh concern) or restructure so no callback is needed. Problem 3 (the design question): keep page.tsx a Server Component. It fetches `metrics` close to the data source with request-scoped access to `db`, and passes plain serializable data down. Marking the whole page 'use client' because two leaves are interactive would move data fetching and the entire import graph into the client bundle, which is also why the bundle grew. Problem 4 (optional): if `db.metrics.findMany()` is slow, wrap Chart in a Suspense boundary near that work, or use the segment's loading boundary, so the shell streams first and the chart reveals independently. Sources: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/server-and-client-boundary.
rubric: Adds 'use client' to the interactive leaf (Chart) and explains the directive as a module-graph boundary, not browser-only rendering.
Identifies the function prop as non-serializable across the boundary and offers a Server Function ('use server') or client-side revalidation as the legal crossing.
Keeps the page a Server Component with data fetching near the source, and resists marking the route client just to serve two interactive leaves.
Reasons about bundle cost: directive placement determines which imports ship to the browser, explaining the oversized bundle.
Optional: adds a Suspense or loading boundary for the slow metrics so the shell streams and the chart reveals independently.

scenarios.prompt: This rename flow ships as a Server Function called from a client form. Review it as you would a public endpoint: list the defects in severity order, explain the attack each one enables, and rewrite the function so the checklist passes. Keep the client form as it is.
rubric: Treats the Server Function as a public endpoint and rejects the client-supplied `userId` as identity.
Authorizes against the specific `projectId` (ownership/tenant), not just "is logged in".
Validates and normalizes input before the write.
Returns a minimal serializable DTO instead of the raw database row.
Revalidates the affected data after the mutation and does not rely on `proxy` for protection.

scenarios.prompt: This root layout fails at request time with `Error: Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components`. Which value crosses the boundary and why is the error unavoidable as written? Then refactor so the theme can change in the browser while the layout stays a Server Component and the pages below stay server-rendered. Explain what happens to `children`.
rubric: Names `onChange` specifically and explains that props crossing into a `'use client'` module must be serializable.
Recognizes a Server Function reference (imported) as the supported client-to-server call, not an inline closure.
Keeps the client boundary at the provider and explains that `children` stay server-rendered.
Separates client state ownership from server persistence instead of moving data fetching to the client.
Rejects the 'make the layout `'use client'`' shortcut and says what it costs.
